newsitem.title: USA: Ex-girlfriend says she dumped Simpson by phone.
newsitem.headline: Ex-girlfriend says she dumped Simpson by phone.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's ex-girlfriend said Wednesday that she broke off their romance by leaving a phone message for him just hours before his former wife and a friend were murdered.

Giving videotaped testimony in the civil trial, model Paula Barbieri said she had then flown to Las Vegas and did not respond to several phone messages the ex-football star left on her answering machine on June 12, 1994.
Later that night, Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were slashed to death at the home of Simpson's ex-wife.

Asked what she had told Simpson, whom she had been dating again since April, 1994, after breaking up with him the previous year, Barbieri said that she had left a message "on his car phone, ending the relationship" at about 7 a.m. that morning.
"Something about (how) we were talking the night before about filling the house with babies and what was wrong and what was wrong now," Barbieri said.

Speaking in a sometimes faltering voice, the elegant model denied the two had had a fight the night before, but said she was upset with him because she was still going through the "healing process" from their first breakup.
Simpson was acquitted in a criminal trial last year of the two murders but is now being sued by the victims' families for "wrongful death".
At his criminal trial, the prosecution had theorised that Simpson snapped emotionally after Barbieri broke off their relationship.
In earlier testimony Wednesday, a volunteer at a shelter for battered women testified that a woman named Nicole called her five days before Simpson's ex-wife was killed, fearing for her life.

Nancy Ney, who was answering hotline phone calls for Los Angeles' Sojourn House in June 1994, said she now believes the woman who complained her ex-husband was stalking and threatening her was Nicole Brown Simpson.
"She said he (her unidentified ex-husband) told her a few different times that if he ever caught her with another man, he would kill her," she said.
Ney said the woman was the same age as Nicole Brown Simpson, with two young children and with a "high-profile" ex-husband, to whom she had been married eight years.
She said the voice on the phone was consistent with Nicole Brown Simpson's voice on a tape of a call to police in 1993.
Defence attorneys earlier tried to block Ney from testifying, arguing that the woman caller was never positively identified as Nicole Brown Simpson.
Ney, who was not allowed to testify during the criminal trial, told jurors that the woman named Nicole called the shelter because she was "frightened" of her ex-husband.
"Her ex-husband had been calling her on the phone and begging her to please come back to him," Ney said. "She said he had been stalking her."
Ney said the caller told her that her ex-husband would show up in restaurants where she was dining and would often be behind her when she looked in her car's rear-view mirror.
"She told me that his behaviour frightened her to such an extent that she was asking my opinion whether I thought it would be safer for her and her children to move back in with him."
At the end of the conversation, Ney said, "we came to the conclusion that in the long run it would not be in her best interest to move back in."

On cross-examination by Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, Ney conceded that, consistent with the shelter's policy, she never asked the woman for her last name, and she acknowledged that a form she filled out during the call did not contain an age or ethnicity for the woman.
Ney was followed on the witness stand Wednesday by Ron Fischman, a friend of Simpson's who saw the former football star several hours before the murders at a dance recital.
Fischman testified that Simpson was "very subdued and quiet" during the recital, which was "not his normal state."
